questions.question: How do you declare and initialize an array in Java, and what are the default values?
questions.title: Array Declaration and Initialization in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Declaration**: `int[] arr;` — just tells Java the type. **Initialization**: `arr = new int[5];` — creates the array with 5 slots. Default values are automatically assigned: `0` for numeric types, `false` for boolean, `null` for objects. You can also declare and initialize in one line with values: `int[] arr = {1, 2, 3};`

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic array syntax and Java's zero-initialization behavior
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting that arrays are objects in Java and go on the heap, or not knowing default values (expecting garbage values like C)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that arrays are objects allocated on the heap, that the length is fixed at creation time, and that Java initializes all array elements to defaults (unlike C/C++)

sections.title: Array Declaration, Initialization, and Defaults
Key Points
sections.content:
- Arrays are **objects** in Java — stored on the heap, accessed via reference
- Length is **fixed** at creation — you can't resize an array
- Default values: `0` (int/byte/short/long), `0.0` (float/double), `false` (boolean), `null` (objects/Strings)
- `array.length` is a **field**, not a method — no parentheses (unlike `String.length()`)
- Index starts at 0; accessing index >= length throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`
- Array literal `{1, 2, 3}` syntax only works at declaration — not for reassignment

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: In Java, you declare an array with the type followed by brackets: `int[] arr`. To create it, you use `new int[5]` which allocates space for 5 integers. One important difference from C: Java automatically initializes all array elements to their default values — zeros for numbers, false for booleans, null for objects. You never get garbage values. If you want to initialize with specific values, you use the array literal syntax: `int[] arr = {1, 2, 3}`. Two things to remember: `array.length` is a field not a method, and the array size is fixed — you can't add more elements later without creating a new array.

questions.question: What are the most useful methods in Java's Arrays utility class?
questions.title: Java Arrays Utility Class — sort, fill, copyOf, toString
questions.direct_answer: The **`java.util.Arrays`** class provides key utility methods: `Arrays.sort(arr)` for sorting, `Arrays.fill(arr, val)` to fill all elements, `Arrays.copyOf(arr, len)` to copy with new size, `Arrays.toString(arr)` to print as a string, and `Arrays.equals(a, b)` to compare two arrays element by element.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of standard library utilities — shows the candidate writes production-level Java, not reinventing the wheel
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing Arrays.toString() for printing arrays — using System.out.println(arr) directly gives a useless memory address
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Arrays.sort uses dual-pivot quicksort for primitives and TimSort for objects, and that printing an array with println directly gives a [I@hashcode format

sections.title: Arrays Utility Methods
Key Points
sections.content:
- `Arrays.toString(arr)` — prints content; `println(arr)` directly prints hash code
- `Arrays.sort(arr)` — sorts in place, O(n log n)
- `Arrays.fill(arr, value)` — sets all elements to the same value
- `Arrays.copyOf(arr, newLength)` — creates a copy with specified length
- `Arrays.equals(a, b)` — compares content; `a == b` just compares references
- `Arrays.binarySearch(arr, key)` — fast search on a SORTED array
- For 2D arrays, use `Arrays.deepToString(arr)` for printing

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The java.util.Arrays class is your toolkit for array operations. The most important ones to know: `Arrays.sort()` sorts the array in place. `Arrays.toString()` converts it to a readable string — this is crucial because if you just pass an array to println directly, you get something like `[I@7852e922` which is the memory address, not the values. `Arrays.fill()` sets all elements to the same value. `Arrays.copyOf()` creates a copy with potentially different size. And `Arrays.equals()` compares two arrays element by element — using `==` on two arrays just checks if they're the same object.

questions.question: What are jagged arrays in Java and how are they different from 2D arrays?
questions.title: Jagged Arrays in Java — Array of Arrays
questions.direct_answer: A **jagged array** (array of arrays) is a 2D array where each row can have a **different length**, unlike a rectangular 2D array where all rows are the same length. In Java, multidimensional arrays are just arrays of arrays, so each row is an independent object with its own length.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Java's array-of-arrays model — shows deeper knowledge than just basic syntax
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking Java 2D arrays always have equal row lengths — they don't have to
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why jagged arrays exist — each row is truly an independent array object, so you allocate rows separately and can make them any size

sections.title: 2D Arrays and Jagged Arrays
Key Points
sections.content:
- Java's `int[][]` is not a true 2D matrix — it's an array of int arrays
- Each row is an **independent array object** with its own length
- Jagged arrays can save memory when rows have very different sizes
- Access: `matrix[row][col]` — rows first, then columns
- `matrix.length` = number of rows; `matrix[i].length` = number of columns in row i
- Use case: Pascal's triangle, representing triangular/variable data

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: In Java, a 2D array is really just an array of arrays — each row is its own independent array object. This means rows don't have to be the same length, which is what we call a jagged array. You create one by declaring the outer array size first, then allocating each row separately with whatever length you need. The practical benefit is memory efficiency when your data is naturally triangular or variable — like a Pascal's triangle. To get the length of a specific row, you use `array[i].length` since each row is its own array with its own length property.

questions.question: What is ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException and how do you prevent it?
questions.title: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException in Java
questions.direct_answer: **`ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`** is thrown when you access an array with an index less than 0 or greater than or equal to the array's length. It's a runtime exception — Java checks bounds at runtime. Prevent it by always validating indices and using `arr.length - 1` as the maximum valid index.

interviewer_intent.testing: One of the most common runtime errors in Java — every developer encounters it
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Accessing index == arr.length (off-by-one) — the last valid index is arr.length - 1, not arr.length
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the off-by-one error as the most common cause, and that for-each loops prevent this entirely by not using indices

sections.title: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
Key Points
sections.content:
- Valid indices: `0` to `arr.length - 1`
- Thrown for: negative indices, index >= length
- It's an **unchecked** (runtime) exception — compiler doesn't force you to handle it
- Off-by-one error: using `i <= arr.length` instead of `i < arr.length` in a loop
- For-each loop automatically avoids index errors (no index to get wrong)
- Unlike C, Java always checks bounds — no silent buffer overflow behavior

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException is thrown whenever you access an array with an invalid index — either negative, or at or beyond the array's length. The last valid index is `arr.length - 1`, not `arr.length`. The most common cause is the classic off-by-one bug in for loops: writing `i <= arr.length` instead of `i < arr.length`. The simplest way to avoid it entirely is to use the enhanced for-each loop when you just need to iterate — then there's no index to mess up. Unlike C, Java always checks array bounds at runtime, so you can never accidentally read past the end of an array without getting an exception.

questions.question: What is the difference between an array and an ArrayList in Java?
questions.title: Array vs ArrayList in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Arrays** have fixed size set at creation and can hold primitives directly. **`ArrayList`** is a resizable list backed by an array that auto-grows, can only hold objects (not primitives), and provides a rich API. Use arrays when size is fixed and performance matters; use ArrayList when size varies.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of when to use each data structure — a fundamental design decision
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Always using ArrayList out of habit when an array would be more appropriate, or thinking ArrayList can hold int directly (it uses Integer autoboxing)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that ArrayList has O(1) amortized add but O(n) insert at position, and that arrays are more memory-efficient for fixed-size collections

sections.title: Array vs ArrayList
sections.content:
| Aspect | Array | ArrayList |
|---|---|---|
| Size | Fixed at creation | Dynamic (auto-resizes) |
| Primitives | Yes (int[], double[]) | No (uses Integer, Double) |
| Syntax | arr[0] | list.get(0) |
| Length/Size | arr.length | list.size() |
| Performance | Faster, less overhead | Slightly slower (boxing/unboxing) |
| Built-in methods | Arrays.sort(), Arrays.fill() | add(), remove(), contains(), sort() |
| Memory | Compact | Has overhead for capacity management |

sections.title: When to Use Each
How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The key difference is resizability. Arrays are fixed-size — once you create an array of 5 elements, it stays 5. ArrayList grows automatically as you add elements. Arrays can store primitives directly like int[] or double[], while ArrayList can only hold objects, so it uses Integer and Double wrapper classes with autoboxing. If you know the size upfront and don't need to add or remove elements, an array is more memory-efficient and slightly faster. If you're building something where the size isn't known in advance, or you need methods like contains() or remove(), ArrayList is the better choice.

questions.question: How do you pass an array to a method in Java — is it pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?
questions.title: Passing Arrays to Methods in Java — Reference Semantics
questions.direct_answer: Java is always **pass-by-value**, but when you pass an array to a method, the value being copied is the **reference** (memory address) to the array. This means the method receives a copy of the reference pointing to the same array — so modifications to the array's elements inside the method affect the original array.

interviewer_intent.testing: A classic Java interview topic — understanding that Java passes object references by value
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking Java passes objects by reference (it doesn't — it passes the reference's value), or thinking array modifications in a method don't affect the caller
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish between modifying array elements (affects caller) vs reassigning the array variable itself (doesn't affect caller)

sections.title: Array Passing — Reference Copy
Key Points
sections.content:
- Java always passes by **value** — for objects/arrays, the value IS the reference
- The method gets a copy of the reference pointing to the SAME array
- Modifying `arr[i]` inside the method changes the original array
- Reassigning `arr = new int[5]` only changes the local copy of the reference
- This is true for all objects, not just arrays
- To prevent a method from modifying your array: pass a copy using `Arrays.copyOf()`

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Java is always pass-by-value. But when you pass an array — or any object — the 'value' being passed is a reference to the array in memory. So the method gets its own copy of the reference, but both the caller's variable and the method's variable are pointing to the same array. This means if the method modifies elements — like `arr[0] = 99` — those changes are visible to the caller. But if the method does `arr = new int[5]`, that just updates the method's local reference; the caller's reference is unaffected and still points to the original array. If you want to prevent a method from modifying your array, pass `Arrays.copyOf(arr, arr.length)` instead.
